title: The Buffalo Nobody Could Fight
tease: No god can beat him alone. So they each give up a piece of what they have, and something walks out of the pile that none of them expected.

source.traditionNote: The Devī Māhātmya is recited whole during Navarātri and is unusually stable — the assembling, the arming and the laugh are in every recension, in that order.
checkedAgainst: Devī Māhātmya — Coburn, 'Encountering the Goddess', SUNY

sourcing.claim: Mahiṣāsura's boon: he cannot be killed by man or god
He defeats the gods and occupies heaven
The gods' anger issues as light, which combines into a single mass
The Devī emerges from that combined light
Each god gives her a weapon drawn from his own
Mahiṣāsura changes form repeatedly during the battle and is killed

audience.careNote: A battle over nine nights, ending in a death. Told the way the Devī Māhātmya tells it — grand rather than gory. Nobody is tortured and nothing lingers. The nine nights of Navarātri are these nine nights, which is usually the thing children most want explained.

values: made out of what everyone had left

blocks.text: «Mahiṣāsura» asked for a clever protection. He did not ask to live forever. He asked that no man and no god should be able to kill him. The boon was granted, and he believed he had closed every path to defeat.
So he took heaven, the way you take a house. He drove the gods out of their own places, and they went and stood outside with a problem none of them could solve alone.

They ended up in front of «Viṣṇu» and «Śiva», telling the story and getting angrier as they told it. No god could simply attack «Mahiṣāsura» and ignore the boon. Their anger came out of them as light instead.
The story says the light was real. It poured from the gods standing there and did not scatter. The lights joined together, brighter and brighter, until they burned like a mountain in front of them.
And from that gathered light a woman emerged — the Devī, formed from the power none of them could use successfully on its own.
Then they armed her. «Śiva» gave his trident, «Viṣṇu» his discus, «Indra» his thunderbolt, and the other gods gave weapons of their own. Himavat, the mountain, gave her a lion to ride.
She stood there holding all of it, looked at the gods who had armed her, and laughed. The story says the world shook, the sea moved, and the mountains trembled at the sound.

The battle lasted through nine nights. «Mahiṣāsura» changed shape again and again — buffalo, lion, man, elephant, buffalo once more. On the tenth morning he was defeated, and the gods could return to heaven.

No single god had been able to solve the problem alone. They gave their power and weapons into one new form, and the answer to the boon was the woman «Mahiṣāsura» had never thought to fear. His careful protection had left exactly one door open.
Nobody could fight the buffalo demon in the ordinary way. His strength was part of the problem, but the boon was the real lock on the door.
He was very strong, but strength was not the main problem. He had arranged the boon so that the usual defenders of heaven could not be the ones to kill him.
When «Mahiṣāsura» was granted his wish he thought about it properly first. He did not ask to live forever — he knew that never works. He asked that no man and no god should be able to kill him.
And it was granted, because it was cleverly asked, and because nobody in the room thought about it for quite long enough.
So he took heaven and forced the gods out of the places they had ruled.

He took it the way you take a house — he moved in, and the people who had been living there went and stood outside. «Indra» had nowhere to send rain from. «Agni» had no fire to keep. They went down and knocked on doors and were told, politely, that nothing could be done.

It went on for a long time. Long enough that people stopped expecting it to end. The seasons came round wrong, and the offerings went up and landed on nobody, and after a while there were children who had never known it any other way.

They ended up in front of «Viṣṇu» and «Śiva», telling the whole story. The longer they described what had happened, the more their anger grew, because none of their usual weapons could get around the boon.
And then the anger came out of them as light — not as another weapon in one god's hand, but as power leaving all of them at once.

The story is literal about the light. It came from «Śiva», from «Viṣṇu», and from the other gods, and it did not disperse. It gathered into one blazing mass until the radiance looked like a mountain of fire.
And from that gathered light a woman emerged — the Devī, formed from the power none of them could use successfully on its own.
Then they armed her. Each god placed a piece of his own power in her hands, giving up the idea that one of them had to be the hero of the battle.

Śiva gave her his trident — pulled out of his own. Viṣṇu his discus. Indra the thunderbolt he had been so proud of. «Yama» his staff. «Vāyu» a bow and a quiver that did not empty. The mountain gave her a lion to ride.
She stood there with all of it, looked at the gods who had armed her, and laughed. She had what she needed, and the world itself seemed to answer the sound.

She looked at the weapons in her hands and at the gods who had handed them over. The problem was clear: no man and no god could kill «Mahiṣāsura». She was neither the man nor the god his boon had protected him from.
She laughed, and the story says the world shook, the sea moved, and the mountains trembled.
The battle did not end in one strike. It stretched across nine nights.
He came at her as a buffalo, and then as a lion, and then as a man with a sword, and then as an elephant, and then as a buffalo again, which was a mistake.
She did not simply strike once and finish it. She watched «Mahiṣāsura» change from one form to another and answered each form as it came.
The lion was not decorative either. It fought beside her while «Mahiṣāsura» kept changing shape and trying another form.
On the tenth morning it was finished, and heaven was empty again, and the gods went back up and found their things where they had left them.
When the battle was over, the gods could return to heaven. The weapons they had placed in her hands had done what none of them could do alone.

«Durgā» had not appeared from nothing. She had emerged from the power the gods released when none of them could win alone. Their defeat became the condition for a different kind of strength to appear.
«Mahiṣāsura» had carefully ruled out man and god. He had simply never imagined the answer would be her. The loophole in his protection was not weakness; it was the person he had failed to count.

linked.reason: the same Devī, a hundred years later, arriving with vegetables instead of a trident

close.question: Every one of them gave up something they had been keeping. What would you have handed over?
close.seed: Some things can only be done by everyone at once.

ifTheyAsk.a: It is, and the story rather enjoys being one. But look at what the loophole is made of: they could not beat him separately and could beat him together, and she is what together looked like when it stood up. The trick and the point are the same shape.
That is exactly why Navarātri is nine nights, and why the tenth day has its own name. If your family keeps a golu or a pūjā, this is the thing being counted.

She laughed, and the text does not apologise for it. Worth being honest that this is a story that enjoys its battle. It is also careful about two things: she does not start it, and she stops the moment it is done.
